title: Holding the breath
hookLine: he tries stopping the breath; his head roars like a blacksmith's bellows (MN 36)
last: FIVE COMPANIONS — YOU DON'T GO ALONE.

cards: Try to fall asleep by force. Squeeze your eyes shut and command yourself: sleep, now. The harder you push, the more awake you get.
Some things don't respond to force. The wanderer has left his two teachers, and now he tries another method of his time: the hard way.
Some ascetics of his day held that if you pushed the body hard enough, through pain, hunger, stillness, the mind would break through. So he pushes.
He clenches his teeth, presses his tongue to the roof of his mouth, and tries to crush his thoughts by sheer will. Sweat pours from his armpits. Then he tries something harder.

teach.b: The Buddha tells this himself, years later, to a man named Saccaka. He describes what he called the breathless meditation.
He stopped breathing through his mouth and nose, and a loud roaring of winds came out of his ears, like the roar of a blacksmith's bellows. He kept going, and stopped the breath in his ears too.
Then it felt like a strong man was splitting his head with a sharp sword. Then like a tight leather strap wound around his head. Then like a butcher carving up his belly.
Then like his whole body roasting over hot coals. It's a hard passage to hear, and he tells it plainly. Through all of it, he says, his energy was tireless and his mindfulness steady.
He wasn't weak. He wasn't lazy.
But his body was overwrought and could not calm down, worn out by the painful striving. The pain did not take over his mind. It just hurt, and it brought no breakthrough.
The breath meditation he would later teach runs almost the opposite way.
In another sutta, the meditator doesn't hold the breath or push it. Breathing in long, he knows he's breathing in long. Breathing in short, he knows it's short.
The breath is watched, not wrestled.

how: In Buddhist breath meditation (anapanasati), practitioners are taught not to hold or force the breath but to know it as it is, long or short; the Buddha's austerities are remembered as the path he tried and set aside.

o: a vow of silence kept by the forest ascetics
a meditation of stopping the breath by sheer force
a slow breathing exercise that calms the whole body

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: the man the Buddha told this to
watching the breath, not holding it

s: the wanderer gave up the breathless meditation because he was too weak
his energy was strong and his mindfulness steady. the forcing just didn't free him.
in the breath meditation the Buddha later taught, you know the breath as it is
breathing in long, you know it's long; breathing in short, you know it's short.
the Buddha describes the roaring in his ears himself
in MN 36, telling Saccaka about his striving.

games.q: you've stopped the breath and your ears roar like a bellows. your will is strong. what do you do?
o: push harder: stop the breath in the ears too.
games.why: he pushes harder, and the pain gets worse: a sword, a strap, a butcher's knife, hot coals. it hurts, but it doesn't free him.

practice: Let your shoulders drop and take three long, easy breaths, each a little slower than the last, the way a swing slows down on its own; don't push them.
Then stop managing the breath altogether: long or short, deep or shallow, your only job is to notice it. If you catch yourself controlling it, smile, and let go again.

wordCard.voice: Appanaka. The breathless meditation the wanderer forced himself through, and learned from: strong effort, great pain, no freedom.

orig.note: Pali: breathless; the appāṇaka jhāna, the breathless meditation of MN 36.

carryVoice: Your line: forcing isn't finding. Some things don't respond to force, however strong the will. That's day forty-four.

sources.ref: Mahasaccaka Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 36): the breathless meditation
